overview: The imported name Damot, its northern Ethiopian and Eritrean location, and its BCE dates point toward ancient Dʿmt. However, the map’s 300 to 200 BCE interval is later than much of the best-known evidence. This card explains the earlier regional society around Yeha; it does not confirm a Dʿmt kingdom with those exact borders and dates.

periods.title: Earlier monumental Yeha
periods.summary: The great buildings belong mainly to the earlier first millennium BCE, centuries before the imported window.

periods.title: An uncertain imported interval
periods.summary: Excavations reveal changing settlement and local gaps. These map dates cannot establish continuous rule by the earlier dynasty.

sections.title: A society connected across the Red Sea

items.text: South Arabian inscriptions and architecture appear alongside local traditions in the northern highlands. Archaeologist Rodolfo Fattovich emphasized a mosaic of different communities rather than one uniform culture. Connections across the Red Sea shaped this region, but they did not make every settlement identical.

Yeha’s Great Temple, built in the seventh century BCE, was dedicated to Almaqah. Its surviving walls rise about fourteen metres. The building later became a Christian sacred place, so the same imposing stonework has belonged to very different religious settings over its long life.

Grat Beʿal Gibri combined stone masonry with horizontal wooden beams. This system supported a building of several storeys. Engineers reported new structural modelling in September 2026, but its impressive theoretical load capacity does not tell us how many storeys the ancient palace actually had.

Builders used different stones for different jobs. Rubble could come from near Yeha, while the Great Temple’s fine limestone blocks travelled from the Wuqro region, roughly ninety kilometres away in a straight line. A beautiful wall also represents quarrying, transport, planning and many people’s hard work.

Researchers identified a basin cut into rock that stored water from a seasonal stream. They suggest small channels and cisterns could supply local fields without copying South Arabia’s giant dams. Managing a useful supply of water did not always require the biggest possible construction project.

sections.title: What pots can tell us about dinner

items.text: Excavated pottery includes jars, bottles, bowls, cups and lids, with polished surfaces and incised decoration. Some vessels had geometric patterns around their shoulders or necks. These remains preserve choices about storage, serving and appearance even when the names of their makers and users have disappeared.

A 2024 study examined tiny organic traces absorbed into pottery and material surviving inside vessels from Yeha and Melazo. It detected both plant and animal fats. A pot can keep traces of its contents long after the meal is gone: useful evidence for archaeologists, though no complete ancient cookbook.

Some samples contained chemical markers associated with fruit fermentation. The researchers also found a slight predominance of plant-related residues in a group of small serving pots. These clues concern the tested vessels; they do not identify every ingredient or establish what every household ate.

One storage vessel from the palace may have held moringa seed oil. The identification remains tentative and needs further study of local raw materials. Even with that uncertainty, laboratory work can ask surprisingly specific questions about what people once kept on a storeroom shelf.

At Yeha, shafts cut down into rock opened into burial chambers. Several people were buried together, possibly in family groups, with objects placed beside them. These tombs connect the monumental city with relationships between the living and the dead, though archaeologists cannot reconstruct each household from the burials alone.

An altar inscription from Ṣ́ǝrḥan names a woman, Taʿattarat, who dedicated it to the goddess ḏāt Ḥamēn. It also names a ruler and his ancestry. Her appearance in this surviving text adds an individual woman to a record otherwise dominated by kings, buildings and scattered objects.

“𐩨𐩬 𐩨𐩬”, transliterated bn bn, means “son of the son”: a grandson. The phrase occurs in that early first-millennium BCE altar inscription. These are normalized Old South Arabian letters based on the published reading; the carving itself varies some letter directions. Family ancestry could be part of a ruler’s public identity.

ending.text: No securely identified event makes 200 BCE the fall of this polity. A Yeha excavation found a break in occupation before later Aksumite settlement, but that local sequence cannot explain every community’s history. The earlier monumental society changed, while the region continued into new political and religious eras.
